name: Autoregressive policy for sequential number selection
key_paper: Vinyals, O., Fortunato, M., & Jaitly, N. (2015). Pointer Networks. NeurIPS 2015. (Foundational autoregressive set-selection architecture; related: Kool, W. et al. (2019). Attention, Learn to Solve Routing Problems! ICLR 2019 — autoregressive attention policy for combinatorial optimization.)
algorithm_description: An autoregressive policy generates a set of k numbers one element at a time: at step t it samples number a_t from a softmax distribution over all N remaining (unselected) numbers, conditioned on the draw history context and the partial sequence (a_1, ..., a_{t-1}) already chosen. The joint probability of the full set factorizes as prod_{t=1}^{k} pi(a_t | context, a_1, ..., a_{t-1}), breaking the intractable joint distribution over C(N,k) outcomes into k tractable sequential softmax steps. Already-selected indices are masked to zero logit before each softmax, guaranteeing distinctness by construction. At each decoding step the context encoder (e.g., the existing SharedLotteryTransformer) provides a fixed representation of historical draws, while a lightweight decoder RNN or attention head aggregates the partial selection to condition the next-step distribution. Gradient flow is unobstructed through the log-probability sequence because each step is a standard categorical sample, making the architecture compatible with REINFORCE, PPO, or any policy gradient estimator.
action_space_handling: The autoregressive policy avoids representing the full C(N,k) joint action space explicitly. Instead, it decomposes the action into k sequential categorical choices each over at most N values. At step t the effective action space is {1..N} minus already-selected numbers, reducing by 1 each step (50, 49, 48, ... for LottoMax 7-from-50). The factored representation is: pi(a_1, ..., a_k | s) = prod_{t=1}^{k} pi_theta(a_t | s, a_{<t}), where conditioning on a_{<t} is implemented by summing or concatenating learned embeddings of previously selected numbers into the decoder state. This is a factored action space with autoregressive (left-to-right) dependency structure -- a strict superset of the flat independent Bernoulli representation used by vanilla REINFORCE, which cannot model the inter-number conditional structure.
how_combinatorial_output_is_formed: At each of k decoding steps: (1) compute logits over all N numbers from the decoder state; (2) apply a mask setting logits of already-selected numbers to -inf; (3) sample one number from the resulting softmax (or argmax for greedy decoding); (4) append selected number to the partial set and update decoder state. The decoder state at step t is typically a combination of the encoder context vector (from the SharedLotteryTransformer over historical draws) and a summary of previously selected numbers (e.g., sum of number embeddings, or the output of an LSTM/attention decoder). For LottoMax this produces exactly 7 distinct numbers from {1..50} with no post-hoc filtering needed. The masking mechanism is the primary combinatorial constraint enforcement strategy -- it is both differentiable with respect to the logits and exact (zero probability of re-selection).
sequential_generation_strategy: This is the defining sequential generation strategy -- numbers are generated strictly autoregressively, one per step, conditioned on all previously selected numbers. This explicitly models inter-number dependencies: pi(a_2 | a_1) != pi(a_2) in general, allowing the policy to learn that if 7 was selected, selecting 14 or 21 may be more or less likely based on historical co-occurrence patterns. The cost is k forward passes per play (or k parallel decoder steps in a single batched forward pass using causal masking in a transformer decoder). Contrasted with flat multi-hot generation (single forward pass, independent per-number logits, no inter-number conditioning) and diffusion-based approaches (fixed number of denoising steps independent of k). For lottery-nn, k=7 (LottoMax), k=6 (6/49), k=5 (Daily Grand), so the overhead is a constant multiplier of 5-7x over the current single-pass architecture.
gradient_estimator_type: Because each autoregressive step is a categorical sample, discrete-sampling gradient estimators are required. The primary compatible estimators are: (1) REINFORCE / score-function estimator -- log pi(a_1..a_k | s) = sum_{t=1}^{k} log pi(a_t | s, a_{<t}), gradient is R * sum_t grad log pi_t; this is unbiased but high-variance and scales with k (variance sums across steps). (2) PPO with clipped surrogate objective -- treats the full autoregressive sequence as a single action and applies the importance-weight clip; compatible and more stable than REINFORCE. (3) Gumbel-softmax / straight-through at each step -- allows reparameterization gradients through each categorical draw using a continuous relaxation; introduces bias but enables lower-variance end-to-end training. (4) RLOO (leave-one-out baseline) -- uses multiple sampled sequences per context to compute a low-variance baseline without a learned critic, particularly suitable for the small-n regime. The best choice for lottery-nn at n~100 is RLOO or PPO due to variance control on sparse reward.
combinatorial_constraint_enforcement: Autoregressive masking is the native and exact constraint enforcement mechanism: at each step t, the logits vector of length N has already-selected indices set to -inf before softmax, making their softmax probability exactly zero. This guarantees: (1) no duplicate selections, (2) exactly k selections after k steps, (3) the constraint is enforced during both training and inference without rejection sampling or post-hoc filtering. No additional constraint layer is needed. The masking operation is differentiable with respect to the unmasked logits (the gradient passes only through non-masked positions), so backpropagation works correctly through the masked softmax. This is superior to rejection sampling (which can require many retries when k approaches N) and is equivalent in expressiveness to Pointer Network decoding (Vinyals et al. 2015).
sample_efficiency_rating: medium -- The autoregressive policy improves over flat multi-label approaches by modeling inter-number dependencies, which in principle reduces the effective hypothesis space and can improve sample efficiency. However, at n~100 draws, learning meaningful sequential conditional distributions across 7 steps from sparse reward is still challenging. The key advantage over flat REINFORCE is that autoregressive masking prevents combinatorially invalid outputs without wasted gradient signal, and the per-step log-probability decomposition allows credit to be distributed across the k steps within each play. The main sample-efficiency cost is that each play now requires estimating k joint log-probabilities instead of one scalar, which multiplies the variance of the gradient estimator by a factor related to k unless a per-step baseline is used. Sample efficiency is medium compared to the field; for this data regime it is better than flat REINFORCE (rated low) but not as data-efficient as offline RL methods that leverage the full fixed dataset without on-policy restrictions.
regularization_built_in: No regularization is intrinsic to the autoregressive architecture itself -- regularization depends on the training algorithm wrapped around it. Commonly applied alongside autoregressive policies: (1) entropy bonus per decoding step -- add beta * H(pi_t) at each step t to prevent the decoder from collapsing to a deterministic sequence; this is the most important regularizer for the small-n sparse-reward case; (2) decoder dropout on number embeddings and decoder hidden states; (3) weight decay on decoder parameters; (4) label smoothing at each decoding step (treat the hard one-hot target as a soft target, preventing overconfident logits); (5) tied embeddings between the number-embedding lookup and the output projection layer reduce parameter count and act as implicit regularization. The encoder (SharedLotteryTransformer) already uses dropout=0.1 and can be frozen during early autoregressive decoder training to prevent catastrophic forgetting.
known_failure_modes_on_small_data: 1. Order sensitivity / position bias: the autoregressive model may learn to select numbers in a canonical ascending order even when the lottery has no ordering semantics -- the learned conditional pi(a_2 | a_1) may overfit to the training draw ordering rather than true co-occurrence structure. Fix: randomly shuffle target number order during training. 2. Compounding errors across decoding steps: an error at step 1 propagates to all subsequent steps; with sparse reward and n~100 draws, the error signal is too weak to correct early-step biases. 3. Decoder overfitting: the sequential decoder (LSTM or additional attention head) has more parameters than the flat output head, risking overfitting on <200 draws. Fix: freeze or heavily regularize the decoder, share weights between encoder context and decoder. 4. High variance of k-step REINFORCE: summing log-probs over k=7 steps multiplies the variance of the score-function estimator by up to 7x compared to single-step sampling, worsening the already-poor signal in the sparse-reward lottery setting. 5. Mode collapse to a fixed sequence: the decoder can converge to always emitting the same k numbers in the same order if entropy regularization is insufficient.
data_regime_evidence: minimum_training_samples_tested: Vinyals et al. (2015) Pointer Networks trained on synthetic TSP with 1K-1M points per instance -- no validation at n < 200 draw-level samples. Kool et al. (2019) Attention Model for VRP/TSP: trained on 100K-1M random instances. Autoregressive policies for discrete RL (text generation): validated at dataset sizes of 10K-1M sequences (Ranzato et al. 2015, Paulus et al. 2017). No published result validates autoregressive set-selection specifically at n~100 labeled outcomes with sparse binary reward. performance_degradation_curve: [uncertain] -- No published degradation curve for autoregressive policies in the n < 200 sparse-reward combinatorial setting. The theoretical variance of the k-step REINFORCE estimator scales as O(k^2 * var(R) / n), suggesting significant degradation as n decreases below 500. comparison_baseline: In combinatorial optimization tasks, autoregressive attention models outperform flat Bernoulli policies by 10-30% on solution quality (Kool et al. 2019), but these results are on datasets with millions of instances. For lottery-scale n~100, the relative advantage of autoregressive over flat sampling is [uncertain] and may be dominated by variance effects.
convergence_guarantees_small_n: [uncertain] -- No finite-sample convergence guarantees exist specifically for autoregressive policies on k-of-N combinatorial selection with n < 200 sparse-reward episodes. The autoregressive decomposition does not change the fundamental sample complexity of the policy gradient estimator; convergence rates still depend on the variance of the gradient estimator, which increases with k (decoding steps) and with reward sparsity. Asymptotic convergence to a local optimum holds under standard REINFORCE conditions (Robbins-Monro step sizes, ergodic sampling) but these are impractical at n~100. PPO-wrapped autoregressive policies have tighter finite-sample bounds than vanilla REINFORCE (Schulman et al. 2017 monotone improvement guarantee) but still require on-policy sampling. The most relevant finite-sample results are for bandit-style autoregressive decoding (each draw is a single episode), where regret bounds of O(sqrt(k * T)) apply with T draws -- for T=100 this gives O(2.6) regret relative to optimal, which is nontrivial.
reward_distribution_handling: The autoregressive architecture is agnostic to reward distribution -- reward is received once at the end of all k decoding steps (play-level reward). For lottery: the scalar reward R (e.g., number of hits out of 7) is assigned equally across all k decoding steps by scaling each step's REINFORCE gradient by R. The extreme sparsity (95% R=0) means most gradient updates across all 7 decoding steps are zero. Reward shaping options compatible with autoregressive decoding: (1) per-step reward -- after selecting a_t, check if a_t is in the actual draw and give r_t = indicator(a_t in draw); this converts the problem to semi-bandit feedback and provides non-zero signal at the individual number level, dramatically improving efficiency; (2) normalized reward R = hits/k maps to [0,1]; (3) distributional returns are not natively supported but a quantile-regression critic can be added alongside the autoregressive policy. Minimum draws for stable per-step reward learning: estimated 200-400 draws [uncertain], still above the current ~100-draw dataset size.
credit_assignment_granularity: The autoregressive formulation naturally supports number-level credit assignment -- at each decoding step t, if the selected number a_t is in the actual draw result, a per-step reward r_t = 1 can be given; otherwise r_t = 0. This is the semi-bandit feedback model applied autoregressively: instead of one sparse scalar R for the whole play, each of the k steps receives its own binary reward signal. This converts the credit assignment granularity from play-level (one reward for the whole set) to number-level (one reward per step), providing up to k=7 times more signal per draw. The gradient update at step t is: r_t * grad_theta log pi_t(a_t | s, a_{<t}), summed across t. This is a significant advantage over flat multi-hot generation, where per-number credit can only be added as a post-hoc modification to the REINFORCE estimator. The sequential structure makes per-step credit assignment the natural and architecturally consistent choice, directly addressing the primary sample-efficiency bottleneck of the small-draw regime.
diversity_mechanism: Autoregressive sampling is inherently stochastic at each of k steps, providing some diversity by default. Explicit diversity mechanisms compatible with the architecture: (1) per-step entropy bonus -- add beta * H(pi_t) at each decoding step to the reward, preventing the decoder from concentrating on a single number at any step; (2) temperature scaling of each step's softmax (T > 1.0 flattens the distribution, already T=1.2 in the existing predict.py); (3) multi-play generation by independently running the full k-step decoding multiple times, sampling independently at each step -- plays naturally diverge because each step's stochasticity compounds over k steps; (4) explicit Jaccard penalty -- after generating m plays, compute pairwise overlap and subtract from reward if any two plays share more than j numbers; (5) determinantal point process (DPP) over the set of plays for maximum-diversity sub-selection. The compounding randomness of k sequential categorical samples means autoregressive generation naturally produces more diverse plays than single-step flat sampling, without any additional mechanism.
offline_vs_online_rl_compatibility: The autoregressive architecture is a policy parameterization, not a learning algorithm, and is compatible with both offline and online RL depending on the training wrapper. For offline RL (the operationally required mode for lottery): (1) Behavioral Cloning -- train the autoregressive policy to imitate historical draws by maximizing sum_t log pi(a_t | draw_history, a_{<t}) on the ~100 historical draws; no reward signal required, purely supervised; this is a valid offline starting point and can be implemented in ~50 lines using the existing data pipeline. (2) Offline RL (CQL/IQL) -- use historical draws as behavior data; the autoregressive policy is the Actor and a separate Critic estimates Q-values from the fixed dataset; conservative penalty prevents out-of-distribution actions. (3) Online RL -- requires generating plays and waiting for draw outcomes (weekly), then updating; impractical as the sole learning signal but can augment offline pretraining. The offline behavioral cloning initialization is the most practically viable starting point for Phase 2 given the n~100 constraint, followed by fine-tuning with per-step reward when new draws arrive.
key_dependencies: No libraries beyond PyTorch are strictly required. PyTorch builtins used: nn.Embedding (number embeddings), nn.GRU or nn.TransformerDecoderLayer (decoder), torch.distributions.Categorical (per-step sampling), masked_fill_ (masking selected indices). Optional: torchrl (torchrl.modules.MaskedCategorical provides a ready-made masked categorical distribution supporting autoregressive masking). No stable-baselines3, pyro, or nflows required for the core architecture.
estimated_lines_of_code: 200-350 lines of new code: ~80 lines for the autoregressive decoder module (number embedding table, step-by-step GRU or attention decoder, masked softmax); ~60 lines for the autoregressive sampling loop with mask bookkeeping; ~80 lines for the REINFORCE or PPO training loop adapted for k-step sequences and per-step rewards; ~40 lines for behavioral cloning pretraining on historical draws; ~30 lines for integration into main_swarm.py predict and log commands. Excludes boilerplate, logging, and the existing SharedLotteryTransformer encoder (reused as-is).
transfer_learning_compatibility: Fully compatible and strongly motivated. The existing SharedLotteryTransformer encoder produces a fixed-length context representation from the draw history window; the autoregressive decoder is a new lightweight module added on top that consumes this frozen context vector at each decoding step. The encoder weights (jointly trained on all 3 lotteries) are preserved and can be frozen during initial autoregressive decoder training, preventing catastrophic forgetting of the shared backbone. Fine-tuning strategy: (1) Phase 2a -- freeze encoder, train decoder only from behavioral cloning on historical draws (~50 lines, fast convergence); (2) Phase 2b -- unfreeze top 1-2 encoder layers and fine-tune jointly with a reduced learning rate (1e-5) while training decoder with per-step reward signal. The lottery_id embedding already provides lottery-specific conditioning, so the same decoder architecture can be shared across all 3 lotteries with lottery-specific linear projections at the output of each step.
specific_application_in_project: The autoregressive policy would be implemented in Phase 2 as the core Actor architecture for combinatorial play generation, replacing the current single-pass temperature-softmax sampling in src/predict.py. Concretely: (1) a new module src/autoregressive_policy.py (~150 lines) wraps the existing SharedLotteryTransformer encoder and adds a per-step decoder (lightweight GRU or single attention head) with a masked categorical output at each of k steps; (2) behavioral cloning pretraining on historical draws gives the decoder a warm-start that replicates historical draw patterns before any RL fine-tuning; (3) after each weekly draw, main_swarm.py log triggers a per-step reward update using the semi-bandit signal (which of the 7 selected numbers actually appeared); (4) entropy bonus per step prevents mode collapse; (5) all 3 lotteries share the same encoder backbone; per-lottery k and N values (7/50, 6/49, 5/49) are passed as configuration. This is Phase 2 priority after the Thompson sampling bandit (already implemented in src/bandit.py). Starting lottery: LottoMax (most data). The autoregressive policy replaces the current predict.py sampling strategy and provides the structured output needed for the Reflexion critique loop (Phase 2 Technique item).
replaces_or_extends: Replaces -- replaces the single-pass temperature-softmax sampling in src/predict.py with a k-step autoregressive decoder that uses the same SharedLotteryTransformer encoder output as context. The encoder itself is extended (not replaced) by adding a decoder head; the data pipeline, joint training loop in main_swarm.py, and bandit.py remain unchanged.
existing_open_source_implementations: 1. Pointer Networks (Vinyals et al. 2015): original TensorFlow implementation at github.com/vinyals/pointer-network; PyTorch port at github.com/shirgur/PointerNet. 2. Attention Model for combinatorial optimization (Kool et al. 2019): github.com/wouterkool/attention-learn-to-route -- autoregressive attention policy for TSP/VRP in PyTorch, closely analogous to lottery number selection. 3. TorchRL MaskedCategorical: pytorch.org/rl/stable -- built-in support for autoregressive masked sampling with full gradient compatibility. 4. Hugging Face Transformers autoregressive decoding: transformers library implements masked autoregressive generation for all seq2seq models; the generate() API with logits_processor supports custom masking (LogitsProcessor) that can enforce no-repeat constraints -- directly adaptable to number uniqueness constraint. 5. RL4CO (github.com/ai4co/rl4co): library specifically for combinatorial optimization with RL, includes autoregressive attention models for k-of-N selection tasks in PyTorch.
benchmark_results: Pointer Networks (Vinyals et al. 2015): on TSP-20 achieved near-optimal tour length (competitive with dynamic programming) using autoregressive generation, while flat models failed to generalize. Attention Model (Kool et al. 2019): on TSP-100 achieved 0.52% optimality gap vs 5.0% for random insertion, 4.9% for nearest neighbor -- a 9x improvement over non-sequential baselines. For NLP text generation with REINFORCE: autoregressive policies are the dominant approach (>99% of production text generation) with BLEU/ROUGE improvements of 1-5 points over flat generation (Paulus et al. 2017, Rennie et al. 2017). On discrete molecule generation: autoregressive graph generation (Jin et al. 2018) outperforms flat generation by 20-40% on validity rate (proportion of chemically valid molecules). No benchmark exists for autoregressive policy on lottery-scale (n~100, sparse reward) set generation tasks as of 2025.
notable_use_cases: 1. Neural combinatorial optimization (TSP, VRP, knapsack): autoregressive attention policies are state-of-the-art for selecting k cities/items from N candidates (Vinyals 2015, Kool 2019, Kwon 2020 POMO) -- structurally identical to selecting k numbers from N. 2. Top-k item recommendation: autoregressive selection of k recommended items from a product catalog (Ie et al. SlateQ 2019, Chen et al. 2019) -- same k-of-N combinatorial structure, similar sparse reward (did the user click?). 3. Drug candidate generation: autoregressive selection of molecular substructures from a fixed vocabulary to form valid molecules (Jin et al. JT-VAE 2018, You et al. GCPN 2018) -- fixed vocabulary of N fragments, select k to form a valid compound; very close structural analog. 4. Code generation and program synthesis: autoregressive generation of API call sequences from a fixed library (requires selecting from N tokens with no-repeat constraints in certain modes) -- demonstrates that autoregressive masking works at scale in production. 5. Multi-label text classification with RL: autoregressive label sequence prediction (Yang et al. 2018, SGM) outperforms flat multi-label prediction by modeling label co-occurrence dependencies -- analogous to number co-occurrence modeling in lottery generation.
